To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the C-terminal tails from HSP90 and HSP70 bind to SPAG1-1TPR1 in a similar way and that the residues of the TPR sequence that interact with the chapeones are conserved.
the TPR1 domain of SPAG1 can bind HSPs with a similar affinity as the wild-type protein.
the first TPR of the human SPAP1 protein binds the C-terminal tails from HSP70 and the N-terminal tail from HSP90, with a preference for the latter.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optimization of a TPR domain and its interaction with the C-terminal tails from HSP70 and from HSP90.
the identification of protein-protein interactions and their modulation by small organic molecules.
the structural and functional characterization of TPR domains, with the aim of understanding their role in macromolecular assemblies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TPR domains have a very high degree of plasticity and can accommodate a wide variety of peptides, but the binding of the peptide is driven by a small number of motifs in the TPr sequences.
the HSP70 binding site in SPAG1 is located at the end of the helix α2 and the beginning of α3, while HSP90 binds to the beginning of helix α3.
, in order to optimize the interaction with HSPs, the C-terminal tail of the HSP should be long enough to allow a strong interaction with the TPR domain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the C-terminal tail of the HSPs is the key element for the interaction, and that the TPR domain can be seen as an adapter for the HSPs.
the C-terminal tails bind to the TPR domain in a similar way to the way they bind HSP90.
we have optimized the first TPR of the human SPAC protein and that this has provided us with insight into how the HSPs bind to it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the TPR domain of SPAG1 can bind HSP70 and, with a higher affinity, HSP90.

, for the first TPR of the SPAG1 protein, the C-terminal tail of HSPs binds the TPR domain through a combination of interactions, with the C-terminal part of the tail interacting with a hydrophobic groove on the surface of the TPR domain, and the N-terminal part of the C-terminal tail interacting with the concave surface of the TTR domain.
the HSPs bind to TPR domains in a very different way than what was previously thought.
